items.name: Linguistics -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
Deciding between inheritance and contact is not a matter of counting resemblances but of asking which domain of the language the resemblances occupy and whether they are recurrent and systematic. The comparative method establishes common descent through regular, recurrent sound correspondences in basic vocabulary. Its probative force follows from a well-attested asymmetry in borrowability: core vocabulary such as body-part terms and low numerals resists borrowing more strongly than cultural vocabulary. Numerals are the most frequently borrowed word class in the world's languages, and that ranking cannot both hold and leave standing the special resilience of low numerals just described; one of the two assessments of numeral stability has to give way.

Grammar, by comparison, is a poor genealogical witness, because structure can be acquired from neighbours as readily as it is inherited from ancestors. Typological traits such as verb-final word order spread easily between languages in contact, and this ready diffusion brings into being a Sprachbund, that is, an area in which languages of different families converge structurally through prolonged contact. The Balkan Sprachbund languages share loss of the infinitive and a postposed definite article. Albanian, Romanian, Greek and Bulgarian belong to separate branches of Indo-European. These same languages descend from a reconstructed Proto-Balkan ancestor dated to the first millennium BCE, a pedigree that cannot be squared with their dispersal across distinct branches of the family, since the two accounts of their common grammar cannot both be correct.

The long-running Altaic controversy illustrates how the two scenarios are weighed against each other. Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic share vowel harmony, suffixing agglutination and verb-final clause order; the proposed Altaic lexical matches, by contrast, cluster in cultural vocabulary such as horse-husbandry and metallurgy terms. That distribution of the lexical evidence indicates transmission between neighbouring speech communities rather than inheritance from a single parent, and a 2003 handbook survey of language contact, appearing some years after the term metatypy had entered the literature, concluded that the Turkic–Mongolic–Tungusic resemblances arose through areal convergence rather than common descent. Structural traits of precisely that kind pass easily across family boundaries, so their recurrence carries little weight once the vocabulary points elsewhere.

A single well-documented case shows what decisive evidence looks like. Takia, an Oceanic language of Karkar Island, has a syntax closely parallel to that of the Papuan language Waskia, and it was this parallelism that led Malcolm Ross to coin the term metatypy for contact-induced restructuring of morphosyntax on the model of a neighbouring language. That syntactic alignment stands in sharp contrast with the lexical picture: Takia retains Proto-Oceanic cognate forms in its basic vocabulary and its pronoun paradigm. The dispute is therefore settled by the stratification of the evidence rather than by the sheer number of shared features, since the inherited pronominal and basic-lexical core fixes the genealogical affiliation while the restructured clause grammar records the history of contact.
